title: CIA hit by hack impacting unclassified information | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence suffered an apparent hack affecting unclassified information, four sources familiar with the matter told CNN.

The intrusion hit a system the agencies draw on​ for open-source intelligence analysis, one of the sources said.

The full extent of the breach was unclear, but officials emphasized that no classified information was affected. “There have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems,” an ODNI official told CNN.

The CIA declined to comment.

Early indications suggest the hack may have originated in China, though it was not immediately clear if the country’s government was involved, two sources said.

It was not immediately clear when the hack occurred or if it has been resolved.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), which oversees 17 US intelligence agencies, including the CIA, has in recent years invested in open-source intelligence work, which is often unclassified.

The apparent intrusion, which the New York Timesfirst reported, is the latest in a string of cybersecurity incidents or tech outages that have rattled the US government and private sector.

The incident does not appear to be related to an apparent hack of the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, two of the sources said, whichCNN first reportedon Friday.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network also said in an alert on its website this week that it was “investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.”

The agency has taken some of its systems offline as a result. It was unclear, however, if the incident was connected to the CIA hack.

The hacking incidents have coincided with aseries of unrelated high-profile tech outagesaffecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system that have rattled Americans’ confidence in the technology that underpins their lives.

Allflights nationwide were groundedfor hours earlier this month after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.

Separately, an outage affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access staples of work life like Outlook email accounts and Teams meetings.

But it’s the disruption at the NSA, the US’ signals intelligence spy agency, and intrusions at the FBI and CIA that have national security officials on alert.

The highly classified network that the NSA uses for its internal communications went down for multiple days last week, CNN firstreported. The apparent cause was a software update gone wrong and not a cyberattack, the nation’s spy chief Jay Clayton said. A critical Georgia facility that supports signals intelligence and cybersecurity operations focused on the Middle East, where the US is currently engaged in a war with Iran was also impacted, CNNreported.

The NSA’s most sensitive and important intelligence-gathering systems were unaffected by the outage, and by Friday, the outage was resolved.

The software vulnerabilities that the NSA was addressing are just a handful in a slew of new vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence has been able to locate. Cybersecurity experts say government agencies and companies alike are discovering a spate of new software bugs in their systems thanks to AI, prompting a rush to fix them and sometimes mistakes along the way.

This story has been updated with additional information.
